_readme: Linguistic Pattern Catalog. Each rule follows the ten fields of thesis Table 13 and is evaluated as D(s,r) = L(s,r) AND S(s,r) AND C(s,r) (FR-DET-03): the lexicalTrigger generates a candidate; it is flagged only if the linguisticCondition (structure/POS) and the contextCondition (local context) also hold. A lexical-only run (L alone) is the section 8.3 baseline. Overlaps are resolved by FR-DET-04: longest span, then higher confidenceTier, then earliest offset, then lowest id. Edit this file to change detection without rebuilding the extension. REPETITION has no rules: it needs a repeated-expression comparison rather than a lexical trigger. Rule ID prefixes of the original seed rules (LL/PS/SC/AF/EM) are legacy names; `technique` is authoritative. confidenceTier is currently authored, not yet calibrated on the development corpus (thesis Stage 5).

_schema.Linguistic Condition: linguisticCondition { type, ... } (types: none, all, any, not, taggedAny, precedesNoun, followedByTag, precededByTag, followedByWord, reportingVerb, inQuestion)
_schema.Context Condition: contextCondition { excludeNeighborWords, excludeWindowWords, excludeSentenceWords, requireSentenceWords, requireNoQuantity, excludeFollowingPattern }
_schema.Target Span: targetSpan ("trigger": the matched word/phrase is the highlighted span)
_schema.Quoted Speech: optional `flagInsideQuotes` (true = still flag when inside quotation marks; default false). Quoted speech is otherwise skipped.

LOADED_LANGUAGE.label: Loaded Language
LOADED_LANGUAGE.description: Words or phrases carrying strong emotional or evaluative implications intended to influence the audience.

NAME_CALLING_LABELING.label: Name Calling / Labeling
NAME_CALLING_LABELING.description: Assigning a person, group, institution, or entity a label associated with something the audience may fear, dislike, admire, or favor.

REPETITION.label: Repetition
REPETITION.description: Repeated use of a word, phrase, message, or idea to increase its persuasive effect.

EXAGGERATION_MINIMIZATION.label: Exaggeration / Minimization
EXAGGERATION_MINIMIZATION.description: Presenting something as substantially greater or less important, serious, significant, or consequential than warranted by the context.

DOUBT.label: Doubt
DOUBT.description: Questioning or undermining the credibility, legitimacy, truthfulness, or reliability of a person, claim, or institution.

APPEAL_TO_FEAR_PREJUDICE.label: Appeal to Fear / Prejudice
APPEAL_TO_FEAR_PREJUDICE.description: Attempting to influence an audience by invoking fear, anxiety, panic, or preconceived judgments.

FLAG_WAVING.label: Flag-Waving
FLAG_WAVING.description: Invoking national, cultural, religious, ideological, or group identity to encourage support for an action, position, or cause.

CAUSAL_OVERSIMPLIFICATION.label: Causal Oversimplification
CAUSAL_OVERSIMPLIFICATION.description: Presenting a complex situation as having a single or substantially simplified cause, including forms of scapegoating.

SLOGANS.label: Slogans
SLOGANS.description: Short, memorable, and striking expressions designed to convey or reinforce a particular message or position.

APPEAL_TO_AUTHORITY.label: Appeal to Authority
APPEAL_TO_AUTHORITY.description: Presenting a claim as true or valid primarily because an authority, expert, institution, or other perceived source supports it.

BLACK_AND_WHITE_FALLACY.label: Black-and-White Fallacy
BLACK_AND_WHITE_FALLACY.description: Presenting an issue as having only two alternatives or reducing a complex situation to opposing choices.

THOUGHT_TERMINATING_CLICHES.label: Thought-Terminating Clichés
THOUGHT_TERMINATING_CLICHES.description: Using familiar or simplified expressions that discourage further examination or critical consideration of an issue.

BANDWAGON_REDUCTIO_AD_HITLERUM.label: Bandwagon / Reductio ad Hitlerum
BANDWAGON_REDUCTIO_AD_HITLERUM.description: Using popularity, social acceptance, or association with a strongly rejected figure or group as a persuasive device.

STRAW_MAN_WHATABOUTISM_RED_HERRING.label: Straw Men / Whataboutism / Red Herring
STRAW_MAN_WHATABOUTISM_RED_HERRING.description: Diverting attention from an issue through misrepresentation of an opposing position, accusations of hypocrisy, or irrelevant alternative issues.

patterns.label: Charged political labeling
patterns.referenceDefinition: Words or phrases carrying strong emotional or evaluative implications intended to influence the audience.

linguisticCondition.description: The word directly modifies a following noun in the same sentence (e.g. 'radical faction').

contextCondition.description: Not a neutral technical collocation such as 'radical surgery' or 'radical honesty'. Not part of a capitalized proper name ('Radical Republicans'). Not a description of the size of a change ('a radical change in doctrine'). Calibration round 2.

patterns.explanation: This word casts the person or group in strongly negative, emotionally loaded terms rather than describing their position neutrally.

sourceExample.text: Outrage as Donald Trump suggests injecting disinfectant to kill virus.
sourceExample.triggerEvidence: Named in thesis section 4.5 (radical/extremist/hardline); annotator-flagged in BABE/MBIC (docs/corpus-mined-bias-candidates.json).

patterns.label: Dehumanizing group/actor label
patterns.referenceDefinition: Assigning a person, group, institution, or entity a label associated with something the audience may fear, dislike, admire, or favor.

linguisticCondition.description: The trigger functions as a noun label or an attributive adjective (Compromise tags singular 'a terrorist organization' as Adjective, plural 'terrorists attacked' as Noun).

contextCondition.description: Not a factual designation or event ('terrorist attack', 'a designated terrorist organization', 'most wanted terrorists'). Calibration round 1: these factual uses were the main source of false positives. Not a hyphenated factual compound ('terrorist-launched rocket'). Calibration round 2.

patterns.explanation: This term labels a person or group in starkly negative, delegitimizing terms rather than describing their actions or stated views neutrally.

sourceExample.text: These Hamas sympathizers are nothing but terrorist apologists.
sourceExample.triggerEvidence: Thesis Table 12 (Name Calling example); extremist/terrorist/racist also annotator-flagged in BABE/MBIC.

patterns.techniqueNote: Moved from LOADED_LANGUAGE: assigning a group a feared/disliked label is Name Calling / Labeling in the SemEval taxonomy.

patterns.label: Delegitimizing government label
patterns.referenceDefinition: Assigning a person, group, institution, or entity a label associated with something the audience may fear, dislike, admire, or favor.

linguisticCondition.description: The trigger is a noun.

contextCondition.description: Not the neutral lifestyle/medical sense ('exercise regime') and not a neutral policy compound ('regime change', 'inspection regime', 'sanctions regime'). Calibration round 1: these compounds were the main source of false positives.

patterns.explanation: 'Regime' frames a government as illegitimate or authoritarian, in contrast to neutral terms like 'government' or 'administration'.

sourceExample.text: WHO: Coronavirus emergency is 'Public Enemy Number 1'
sourceExample.triggerEvidence: Authored from the technique definition; the neutral sense is excluded by the context condition.

patterns.techniqueNote: Mapped to NAME_CALLING_LABELING: 'regime' labels a government with a term the audience is primed to dislike.

patterns.label: Combative reporting verb
patterns.referenceDefinition: Words or phrases carrying strong emotional or evaluative implications intended to influence the audience.

linguisticCondition.description: Has a subject before it and an object (or 'at') right after it, i.e. one party criticizing another.

contextCondition.description: Not the physical senses ('slammed the door', 'blasted off').

patterns.explanation: A combative verb that dramatizes disagreement instead of neutrally stating that someone criticized or disagreed.

sourceExample.text: Outrage as Donald Trump suggests injecting disinfectant to kill virus.
sourceExample.triggerEvidence: Observed in a development article (Fox News, 2026-10-02: 'blasts'); 'slammed' (34) and 'blasted' (20) annotator-flagged in BABE/MBIC.

patterns.label: Evaluative adjective
patterns.referenceDefinition: Words or phrases carrying strong emotional or evaluative implications intended to influence the audience.

linguisticCondition.description: An evaluative adjective applied to something: attributive (before a noun) or predicative (after 'is/was').

contextCondition.description: Not a fixed idiom or a weather description ('vicious cycle', 'brutal heat wave').

patterns.explanation: This word states the writer's own emotional judgment instead of describing what happened and letting the reader decide.

sourceExample.text: Israel must defend itself from the barbaric terrorists surrounding its borders.
sourceExample.triggerEvidence: Thesis Table 12 (Loaded Language example); 'bizarre' (22) annotator-flagged in BABE/MBIC.

patterns.label: Reputational judgment modifier
patterns.referenceDefinition: Words or phrases carrying strong emotional or evaluative implications intended to influence the audience.

linguisticCondition.description: The reputational modifier directly precedes the noun it judges (Compromise tags 'disgraced' as a past-tense verb, so the rule keys on the following noun, not the trigger's own tag).

contextCondition.description: Not part of a capitalized name ('The Notorious B.I.G.'). Not describing a disease or pathogen ('one of the most notorious diseases'). Calibration round 2.

patterns.explanation: This word injects the writer's own negative judgment about someone's reputation, rather than letting the reader draw that conclusion from neutrally reported facts.

sourceExample.text: Outrage as Donald Trump suggests injecting disinfectant to kill virus.
sourceExample.triggerEvidence: Cross-validated in BABE/MBIC annotator flags and WNC edit pairs (docs/corpus-mined-bias-candidates.json).

patterns.label: Guilt-presupposing reporting verb
patterns.referenceDefinition: Words or phrases carrying strong emotional or evaluative implications intended to influence the audience.

linguisticCondition.description: Used as a reporting verb: followed by 'that' or an opening quotation mark.

contextCondition.description: Not an unrelated sense ('admitted to the hospital', 'evidence admitted in court').

patterns.explanation: This verb frames the statement as if wrongdoing or a hidden truth is already established, rather than neutrally reporting what the source said (e.g. 'said' or 'stated').

sourceExample.text: Outrage as Donald Trump suggests injecting disinfectant to kill virus.
sourceExample.triggerEvidence: Original thesis seed rule.

patterns.techniqueNote: Mapped to LOADED_LANGUAGE: the SemEval taxonomy has no presupposition class; these reporting verbs carry evaluative implications.

patterns.label: Group/person label
patterns.referenceDefinition: Assigning a person, group, institution, or entity a label associated with something the audience may fear, dislike, admire, or favor.

linguisticCondition.description: The label functions as a noun (or the leading adjective of a two-word label).

contextCondition.description: Not the proper name of an organization ('Democratic Socialists of America', 'Socialist Party'). Not a capitalized party or group name ('Spain's Socialists', 'Thug Life').

patterns.explanation: This is a label for a person or group that the audience is likely to react to emotionally, rather than a neutral description of who they are or what they did.

sourceExample.text: WHO: Coronavirus emergency is 'Public Enemy Number 1'
sourceExample.triggerEvidence: Observed in a development article (Breitbart, 2026-10-02: 'socialists', 'radicals', 'haters', 'Illegals'); illegal (47), aliens (34), leftist (31) annotator-flagged in BABE/MBIC.

patterns.label: Immigration-status label
patterns.referenceDefinition: Assigning a person, group, institution, or entity a label associated with something the audience may fear, dislike, admire, or favor.

linguisticCondition.description: The phrase functions as a label for people.

contextCondition.description: Not when used as the statutory term in legal or enforcement reporting ('an illegal alien with a final order of removal was arrested'). Calibration round 2.

patterns.explanation: This labels people by immigration status in a way widely regarded as dehumanizing, rather than describing them neutrally.

sourceExample.text: Illegals are flooding our borders
sourceExample.triggerEvidence: Split from NC-001 in calibration round 2: 'illegal alien' is also the U.S. statutory term, so legal and enforcement contexts are skipped.

patterns.label: Exaggerating intensifier
patterns.referenceDefinition: Presenting something as substantially greater or less important, serious, significant, or consequential than warranted by the context.

linguisticCondition.description: The intensifier is used as a descriptive word or verb, not as a name.

contextCondition.description: The sentence gives no figure (number, percent, money). A stated quantity substantiates the claim; the SemEval definition concerns magnitude 'greater than warranted by the context'.

patterns.explanation: This word makes something sound larger or more severe than the plain facts may justify. A specific figure is more informative.

sourceExample.text: Coronavirus 'risk to the American people remains very low', Trump said.
sourceExample.triggerEvidence: Observed in a development article (BBC, 2026-10-02: 'skyrocketed'); enormous/crushing annotator-flagged in BABE/MBIC.

patterns.label: Downplaying phrase
patterns.referenceDefinition: Presenting something as substantially greater or less important, serious, significant, or consequential than warranted by the context.

linguisticCondition.description: The downplaying word is followed by the thing being minimized.

contextCondition.description: No additional local context condition. 'merely' was removed in calibration round 2: it is mostly a neutral adverb ('he merely sold the rounds').

patterns.explanation: This phrasing shrinks the importance of something instead of letting the facts show how significant it is.

sourceExample.text: Coronavirus 'risk to the American people remains very low', Trump said.
sourceExample.triggerEvidence: Authored from the technique definition (minimization).

patterns.neutralAlternative: Use the actual figure or fact

patterns.label: Downplaying phrase (fixed)
patterns.referenceDefinition: Presenting something as substantially greater or less important, serious, significant, or consequential than warranted by the context.

lexicalTrigger.pattern: \b(no big deal|not a big deal|barely matters)\b

linguisticCondition.description: The multi-word expression is itself the anchor.

contextCondition.description: No additional local context condition.

patterns.explanation: A stock phrase that waves away an issue's importance instead of showing why it matters little.

sourceExample.text: Coronavirus 'risk to the American people remains very low', Trump said.
sourceExample.triggerEvidence: Authored from the technique definition (minimization).

patterns.neutralAlternative: Give the facts and let readers judge

patterns.label: Doubt-casting qualifier
patterns.referenceDefinition: Questioning or undermining the credibility, legitimacy, truthfulness, or reliability of a person, claim, or institution.

linguisticCondition.description: The qualifier modifies a following noun ('so-called experts').

contextCondition.description: Not when it introduces a quoted term or name ('the so-called "sunset" clause'), where it only names the term. Calibration round 2.

patterns.explanation: This qualifier signals the writer doubts a person, claim, or title without presenting evidence for that doubt.

sourceExample.text: Can the same be said for the Obama Administration?
sourceExample.triggerEvidence: Authored from the technique definition.

patterns.neutralAlternative: Name the person or claim directly

patterns.label: Doubt-casting adverb
patterns.referenceDefinition: Questioning or undermining the credibility, legitimacy, truthfulness, or reliability of a person, claim, or institution.

linguisticCondition.description: The adverb qualifies a verb, adjective or noun that follows.

contextCondition.description: Not legal or incident hedging: no police/court/charge vocabulary and no account of a specific crime or incident ('the gunman allegedly shot...') in the same sentence. Also skipped when the claim is attributed ('according to a neighbor'). Calibration round 1: crime-report uses were the main source of false positives.

patterns.explanation: This adverb casts doubt on a claim without saying why. In crime reporting it is a standard legal hedge, so it is skipped when legal terms appear in the same sentence.

sourceExample.text: Can the same be said for the Obama Administration?
sourceExample.triggerEvidence: Observed in a development article (Fox News, 2026-10-02: 'allegedly linked').

patterns.neutralAlternative: State who alleges it and what the evidence is

patterns.label: Insinuating rhetorical question
patterns.referenceDefinition: Questioning or undermining the credibility, legitimacy, truthfulness, or reliability of a person, claim, or institution.

linguisticCondition.description: The word sits in an interrogative sentence.

contextCondition.description: The question poses a contrast ('X, or are they secretly Y?'), which distinguishes insinuation from a plain question.

patterns.explanation: A question that insinuates hidden motives ('... or are they secretly ...?') raises suspicion without presenting evidence.

sourceExample.text: Are these protesters really demanding human rights, or are they secretly supporting Hamas?
sourceExample.triggerEvidence: Thesis Table 12 (Doubt example); SemEval Table 1 also gives a rhetorical question as the Doubt example.

patterns.neutralAlternative: Report the evidence for or against the motive

patterns.label: Doubt-casting reporting verb
patterns.referenceDefinition: Questioning or undermining the credibility, legitimacy, truthfulness, or reliability of a person, claim, or institution.

linguisticCondition.description: Used as a reporting VERB ('X claimed that ...'): followed by 'that' or a quote, tagged as a verb, and not directly after a determiner, possessive, adjective or preposition. This excludes the noun use ('rejected claims that ...', 'the claims that ...', 'false claims that ...').

contextCondition.description: No additional local context condition.

patterns.explanation: Using 'claim' instead of a neutral verb like 'said' can subtly cast doubt on a source's statement without the writer explicitly saying they doubt it.

sourceExample.text: Can the same be said for the Obama Administration?
sourceExample.triggerEvidence: Annotator-flagged in BABE/MBIC (claim 53, claimed 46, claims 40).

patterns.techniqueNote: Mapped to DOUBT: 'claimed' undermines the credibility of the quoted statement.

patterns.label: Fear-invoking phrase
patterns.referenceDefinition: Attempting to influence an audience by invoking fear, anxiety, panic, or preconceived judgments.

lexicalTrigger.pattern: \b(existential threat|threat to democracy|crime wave|wave of crime|climate of fear|grave danger|mortal danger|deadly threat|terrifying|ticking time bomb|never be safe again|will never be safe|reign of terror|nightmare scenario|doomsday scenario|menace to society|public menace|spiral(?:l?ing|l?ed|s)? out of control)\b

linguisticCondition.description: The multi-word expression is itself the anchor (phrase-level condition).

contextCondition.description: No additional local context condition.

patterns.explanation: This wording is meant to provoke fear or alarm rather than inform; the underlying risk is stated in dramatic terms.

sourceExample.text: If Hamas is not completely defeated, Israeli families will never be safe again.
sourceExample.triggerEvidence: Thesis Table 12 (Appeal to Fear example); other phrases authored from the technique definition.

patterns.neutralAlternative: State the specific risk and its evidence

patterns.label: Fear-invoking figure of speech
patterns.referenceDefinition: Attempting to influence an audience by invoking fear, anxiety, panic, or preconceived judgments.

lexicalTrigger.pattern: \b(under siege|under invasion|being invaded|invaded by|under attack|overrun (?:by|with)|hordes of)\b

linguisticCondition.description: The multi-word expression is itself the anchor.

contextCondition.description: Figurative use only: skipped when the sentence is about an actual military siege or attack ('a village under siege during the war', 'came under attack from gunmen'), a cyberattack, or a literal infestation ('a garden overrun by weeds').

patterns.explanation: Describing something as 'under siege', 'under invasion' or 'overrun' casts it as being attacked, to provoke alarm, rather than stating what actually happened.

sourceExample.text: If Hamas is not completely defeated, Israeli families will never be safe again.
sourceExample.triggerEvidence: Authored from the technique definition; the literal military sense is excluded by the context condition.

patterns.label: Alarmist damage idiom
patterns.referenceDefinition: Attempting to influence an audience by invoking fear, anxiety, panic, or preconceived judgments.

linguisticCondition.description: The multi-word expression is itself the anchor.

contextCondition.description: Skipped in weather and traffic reports, where the idiom describes physical damage that is the news itself ('the storm wreaked havoc on the coast').

patterns.explanation: This idiom predicts dramatic, unspecified damage to provoke alarm instead of stating what harm is expected and how likely it is.

sourceExample.text: Screwworms have the potential to wreak havoc on the Lone Star State.
sourceExample.source: News article reported by the team, 2026-10-13
sourceExample.triggerEvidence: Authored from the technique definition after a missed detection on this sentence; weather use excluded by the context condition.

patterns.neutralAlternative: State the specific expected harm and its likelihood

patterns.label: Identity-appeal phrase
patterns.referenceDefinition: Invoking national, cultural, religious, ideological, or group identity to encourage support for an action, position, or cause.

lexicalTrigger.pattern: \b(true patriots?|real americans?|real patriots?|true supporters?|our way of life|american way of life|our great nation|freedom-loving|god-fearing|for god and country)\b

linguisticCondition.description: The multi-word expression is itself the anchor (phrase-level condition).

contextCondition.description: No additional local context condition.

patterns.explanation: This invokes national or group identity to win support, implying that agreeing is what a loyal member of the group does.

sourceExample.text: True supporters of Israel stand with the IDF.
sourceExample.triggerEvidence: Thesis Table 12 (Flag-Waving example); other phrases authored from the technique definition.

patterns.neutralAlternative: Describe the policy or position itself

patterns.label: Single-cause claim
patterns.referenceDefinition: Presenting a complex situation as having a single or substantially simplified cause, including forms of scapegoating.

lexicalTrigger.pattern: \b(the only reason|the sole reason|the sole cause|solely responsible|entirely to blame|entirely responsible|single cause|all because of|the one reason)\b

linguisticCondition.description: The multi-word expression is itself the anchor (phrase-level condition).

contextCondition.description: Not negated ('it is not the only reason'), which rejects a single cause. Calibration round 2.

patterns.explanation: This presents a complicated situation as having one cause. Most real events have several contributing factors.

sourceExample.text: If France had not have declared war on Germany then World War II would have never happened.
sourceExample.triggerEvidence: Authored from the technique definition (single-cause wording).

patterns.label: Campaign slogan
patterns.referenceDefinition: Short, memorable, and striking expressions designed to convey or reinforce a particular message or position.

lexicalTrigger.pattern: \b(make america great again|build the wall|lock her up|drain the swamp|defund the police|stop the steal|yes we can|hope and change)\b

linguisticCondition.description: The multi-word expression is itself the anchor (phrase-level condition).

contextCondition.description: No additional local context condition.

patterns.explanation: A short, memorable slogan designed to rally support. Quoting it is not wrong, but it carries persuasive framing rather than explanation.

sourceExample.text: "BUILD THE WALL!" Trump tweeted.
sourceExample.triggerEvidence: SemEval Table 1 gives 'BUILD THE WALL!' as the Slogans example; other slogans are well-known campaign slogans.

patterns.neutralAlternative: Explain the policy behind the slogan

patterns.label: Rallying phrase
patterns.referenceDefinition: Short, memorable, and striking expressions designed to convey or reinforce a particular message or position.

linguisticCondition.description: The multi-word expression is itself the anchor.

contextCondition.description: No additional local context condition.

patterns.explanation: A short, forceful phrase designed to rally support rather than explain a position.

sourceExample.text: Israel must win at all costs.
sourceExample.triggerEvidence: Thesis Table 12 (Slogans example).

patterns.neutralAlternative: Explain the position and its trade-offs

patterns.label: Unnamed expert or study
patterns.referenceDefinition: Presenting a claim as true or valid primarily because an authority, expert, institution, or other perceived source supports it.

linguisticCondition.description: The multi-word expression is itself the anchor (phrase-level condition).

contextCondition.description: Not already attributed to a named source in the same sentence ('according to ...', 'the journal reported').

patterns.explanation: This leans on an unnamed authority to make a claim sound settled. Naming the expert or study lets readers check it.

sourceExample.text: ...confirmed that 'Vigan said the truth. That's all.'
sourceExample.triggerEvidence: Observed in a development article (BBC, 2026-10-02: 'experts warn').

patterns.neutralAlternative: Name the specific expert or study

patterns.label: Unattributed collective claim
patterns.referenceDefinition: Presenting a claim as true or valid primarily because an authority, expert, institution, or other perceived source supports it.

linguisticCondition.description: The multi-word expression is itself the anchor (phrase-level condition).

contextCondition.description: No additional local context condition.

patterns.explanation: This attributes a claim to a vague, unnamed group instead of a specific, checkable source, making the claim difficult to verify.

sourceExample.text: ...confirmed that 'Vigan said the truth. That's all.'
sourceExample.triggerEvidence: Original thesis seed rule.

patterns.techniqueNote: Mapped to APPEAL_TO_AUTHORITY (vague/unnamed authority). 'many believe' is arguably Bandwagon; kept in one rule to preserve the original seed phrases.

patterns.label: Either/or framing
patterns.referenceDefinition: Presenting an issue as having only two alternatives or reducing a complex situation to opposing choices.

lexicalTrigger.pattern: \b(with us or against us|no middle ground|only two (?:options|choices|sides)|there is no alternative|no other choice)\b

linguisticCondition.description: The phrase is not immediately followed by a noun ('there is no alternative route' is literal; 'there is no alternative.' is the fallacy).

contextCondition.description: No additional local context condition.

patterns.explanation: This frames the issue as having only two sides, leaving out the range of positions in between.

sourceExample.text: Francis said these words: 'Everyone is guilty for the good he could have done and did not do ... If we do not oppose evil, we tacitly feed it.'
sourceExample.triggerEvidence: Authored from the technique definition.

patterns.label: Either/or demand
patterns.referenceDefinition: Presenting an issue as having only two alternatives or reducing a complex situation to opposing choices.

linguisticCondition.description: An 'or' follows within the sentence, completing the either/or construction.

contextCondition.description: No additional local context condition.

patterns.explanation: This frames the issue as having only two sides, leaving out the range of positions in between.

sourceExample.text: You either support Israel or you support terrorism.
sourceExample.triggerEvidence: Thesis Table 12 (Black-and-White example).

patterns.label: Thought-terminating cliché
patterns.referenceDefinition: Using familiar or simplified expressions that discourage further examination or critical consideration of an issue.

lexicalTrigger.pattern: \b(end of story|end of discussion|it['’]s what it is|it is what it is|case closed|nothing to see here|enough said|that['’]s just the way it is|everything happens for a reason|boys will be boys)\b

linguisticCondition.description: The multi-word expression is itself the anchor (phrase-level condition).

contextCondition.description: No additional local context condition.

patterns.explanation: A stock phrase that signals the discussion is over, discouraging the reader from examining the issue further.

sourceExample.text: Israel has the right to defend itself. End of discussion.
sourceExample.triggerEvidence: Thesis Table 12 (Thought-Terminating Cliche example).

patterns.label: Popularity or Hitler comparison
patterns.referenceDefinition: Using popularity, social acceptance, or association with a strongly rejected figure or group as a persuasive device.

lexicalTrigger.pattern: \b(everyone knows|everybody knows|everyone agrees|everybody agrees|no one disputes|nobody disputes|most people agree|most people believe|the majority agree|millions of (?:people|americans) agree|wrong side of history|like hitler|new hitler|hitler-like|nazi-like)\b

linguisticCondition.description: The multi-word expression is itself the anchor (phrase-level condition).

contextCondition.description: No additional local context condition.

patterns.explanation: This persuades through popularity ('everyone agrees') or by linking someone to a universally rejected figure, rather than through evidence.

sourceExample.text: The whole world now stands with Israel, and anyone who still questions the operation is on the wrong side of history.
sourceExample.triggerEvidence: Thesis Table 12 (Bandwagon example).

patterns.neutralAlternative: Cite the evidence or the actual survey

patterns.label: Whataboutism / diversion
patterns.referenceDefinition: Diverting attention from an issue through misrepresentation of an opposing position, accusations of hypocrisy, or irrelevant alternative issues.

lexicalTrigger.pattern: \b(but what about|and what about|whataboutism|red herring|straw man|why aren['’]t you (?:talking|asking))\b

linguisticCondition.description: The multi-word expression is itself the anchor (phrase-level condition).

contextCondition.description: No additional local context condition.

patterns.explanation: This redirects attention to a different issue or accusation instead of answering the point being discussed.

sourceExample.text: Instead of criticizing Israel, why aren't you talking about what Hamas did?
sourceExample.triggerEvidence: Thesis Table 12 (Whataboutism example).

patterns.label: Absolute or all-time claim
patterns.referenceDefinition: Presenting something as substantially greater or less important, serious, significant, or consequential than warranted by the context.

linguisticCondition.description: The absolute or all-time construction is itself the anchor.

contextCondition.description: Not a measured record backed by figures ('the deadliest storm in history, killing 8,000'), and not a business, product or sports context where the phrase is literal or routine.

patterns.explanation: This presents the issue in absolute, all-time terms (the worst ever, the end of everything) instead of describing its actual size or likely effect.

sourceExample.text: If Israel loses this war, the entire country will cease to exist.
sourceExample.triggerEvidence: Thesis Table 12 (Exaggeration example) and Table 9 ('the greatest threat our civilization has ever faced'); measured records and business/sports uses excluded by the context condition.

patterns.neutralAlternative: Describe the actual scale or likely effect

patterns.label: Single-condition solution
patterns.referenceDefinition: Presenting a complex situation as having a single or substantially simplified cause, including forms of scapegoating.

lexicalTrigger.pattern: \b(?:(?:simply|just|only) (?:surrendered|surrender|resigned|resign|stepped down|step down|gave up|give up|went away|go away|stopped|stop|left|leave)|would be (?:peace|no (?:crime|war|inflation|problem|problems|crisis)) (?:tomorrow|overnight|immediately))\b

linguisticCondition.description: The phrase is itself the anchor.

contextCondition.description: Part of a conditional ('if X simply surrendered'), so a complex outcome is presented as hinging on one actor's single act.

patterns.explanation: This presents a complex situation as if one actor's single act would resolve it, leaving out the other causes involved.

sourceExample.text: There would be peace tomorrow if Hamas simply surrendered.
sourceExample.triggerEvidence: Thesis Table 12 (Causal Oversimplification example).

patterns.label: Authority as a reason not to question
patterns.referenceDefinition: Presenting a claim as true or valid primarily because an authority, expert, institution, or other perceived source supports it.

lexicalTrigger.pattern: \b(?:there is no (?:reason|need) to (?:question|doubt|challenge) (?:it|them|this|that)|who are we to (?:question|doubt|challenge)|(?:we|you) (?:should|must) (?:simply |just )?trust (?:the|our) (?:experts|military|generals|scientists|doctors|leaders|government|officials))\b

linguisticCondition.description: The phrase is itself the anchor.

contextCondition.description: The sentence cites an authority, so the phrase uses that authority as the reason to stop questioning the claim.

patterns.explanation: This treats an authority's statement as a reason to stop questioning the claim, instead of giving the evidence for it.

sourceExample.text: Our military leaders have said the operation is necessary, so there is no reason to question it.
sourceExample.triggerEvidence: Thesis Table 12 (Appeal to Authority example).

patterns.neutralAlternative: State the evidence behind the authority's claim

patterns.label: Flood metaphor for people
patterns.referenceDefinition: Words or phrases carrying strong emotional or evaluative implications intended to influence the audience.

linguisticCondition.description: The metaphor is itself the anchor.

contextCondition.description: About people, not literal water ('rain flooding the streets') or goods, where 'pouring across the border' describes trafficking volumes.

patterns.explanation: This describes people with a flood or swarm metaphor, which frames them as a natural disaster or threat rather than describing who they are and how many.

sourceExample.text: Illegals are flooding our borders
sourceExample.triggerEvidence: Thesis Table 9 (Loaded Language example); literal water and goods/trafficking uses excluded by the context condition.

patterns.neutralAlternative: State who is arriving and in what numbers

patterns.label: Immediate rhetorical repetition
patterns.referenceDefinition: Repeated use of a word, phrase, message, or idea to increase its persuasive effect.

words: take it back! take it back

linguisticCondition.description: The repeated word and the words between its occurrences form the span.

contextCondition.description: A word repeated straight after a comma ('Jobs, jobs, jobs') or a phrase restarted straight after an exclamation mark ('Take our country back! Take it back!'): a rhetorical device rather than ordinary reference. Repetition spread across the whole article is not covered.

patterns.explanation: This repeats the same word or phrase back-to-back to drive the message home through repetition rather than argument.

sourceExample.text: We must take our country back! Take it back!
sourceExample.triggerEvidence: Thesis Table 9 (Repetition example). Only immediate repetition is covered; repetition spread across an article needs article-level comparison (thesis 4.2).
